text: The history of women's cricket dates back to a report in The Reading Mercury on 15 August 1745, describing a match between Bramley and Hambledon near Guildford in Surrey. Early matches were not always formal; for instance, a game on 13 July 1747 at the Artillery Ground between Charlton and Westdean and Chilgrove in Sussex spilled over into the next day due to crowd disturbances. Women's matches were frequently held in Sussex, Hampshire, and Surrey, often in front of large crowds with heavy betting, where single women competed against married women, with prizes including barrels of ale or pairs of lace gloves. The first county match took place in 1811 between Surrey and Hampshire at Ball's Pond in Middlesex, funded by two noblemen with 1,000 guineas, and involved players aged 14 to 60. Cricket deliveries were initially underarm, though roundarm bowling was reportedly pioneered by Christiana Willes in the early 19th century; however, it was actually devised by Tom Walker in the 1790s. The first women's cricket club, the White Heather Club, was formed in 1887 at Nun Appleton in Yorkshire. In 1890, the Original English Lady Cricketers toured England, playing exhibition matches to large crowds and achieving success until their manager absconded with the profits, leading to the team's dissolution. James Lillywhite's Cricketers' Annual for 1890 included a photograph and article on women's cricket, noting that cricket was less severe than lawn tennis and less dangerous than hunting or skating, and thus considered a positive development. The Women's Cricket Association was established in 1926. The England team first played against The Rest at Leicester in 1933 and undertook the first international tour to Australia in 1934–35, playing the first Women's Test match between England and Australia in December 1934, winning two and drawing one. England then traveled to New Zealand, where Betty Snowball scored 189 in the first Test in Christchurch. Barbara Rae was the founder, captain, and top scorer of Australia's first recorded women's cricket match, held on 7 April 1874 in Bendigo, Victoria. Lily Poulett-Harris, a young Tasmanian, captained the Oyster Cove team in the league she founded in 1894 and is credited as the founding mother of women's cricket in Australia; her obituary states her team was likely the first formed in the colonies. The Victoria Women's Cricket Association was founded in 1905 and the Australian Women's Cricket Association in 1931; the current competition is managed by the Women's National Cricket League. The International Women's Cricket Council was formed in 1958 to coordinate women's cricket in Australia, England, New Zealand, South Africa, the West Indies, Denmark, and the Netherlands. Test cricket has been played by Australia, England, India, Ireland, Netherlands, New Zealand, Pakistan, South Africa, Sri Lanka, and the West Indies. A total of 131 women's Test matches have been played, mostly involving England or Australia. Originally three-day matches, most have since 1985 been four-day games. England has played 87 Tests since 1934, winning 19, losing 11, and drawing 57; Australia has played 67, winning 18, losing nine, and drawing 40. Australia's highest total is 569 for six declared against England in 1998; the highest individual score is 242 by Kiran Baluch for Pakistan Women against West Indies Women at the National Stadium, Karachi in 2003/04. Five other women have scored double centuries. Neetu David of India took eight wickets in an innings against England in 1995/56, and seven wickets have fallen to the same bowler on ten occasions. The best match figures, 13 for 226, were recorded by Shaiza Khan for Pakistan Women against West Indies Women in Karachi in 2003/04. Three English batsmen—Janet Brittin (1935 runs at 49.61), Charlotte Edwards (1621 at 49.09), and Rachel Heyhoe-Flint (1594 at 45.54)—lead the all-time run-scoring lists, with six other women scoring over 1,000 Test runs. Mary Duggan of England took 77 Test wickets at 13.49, while Australia's Betty Wilson took 68 at 11.8; seven other women have 50 or more wickets. Betty Wilson was the first player, male or female, to record a century and ten wickets in a Test match, against England at the MCG in 1958. Australia were bowled out for 38 but gained a first-innings lead of three by dismissing England for 35 in reply, with Wilson taking seven for seven. 35 remains the lowest total ever in a women's Test. Australia set England 206 to win, but the visitors held on for a draw. In 1985, Australia's Under-21 National Women's Cricket Championship was renamed the Betty Wilson Shield in her honor. Jan Molyneaux made a record 298 for Olympic v Northcote in Melbourne's A-grade final in 1967 and also scored 252 not out in a 477-run partnership with Dawn Rae. Club and county cricket in England has evolved, with a National Knock-Out Cup and a league structure ending in Northern and Southern Premier Leagues. The major county competition is the LV Women's County Championship, and Super Fours, featuring teams named after precious stones, serves as a bridge between domestic and international elite play. In April 1970, Sian Davies and Sally Slowe of Cheltenham Ladies' College attended MCC's traditional Easter coaching classes at Lord's, breaking the 'gender barrier'. The first Women's Cricket World Cup was held in England in 1973, partially funded by Jack Hayward, and won by the hosts at Lord's in front of Princess Anne. Enid Bakewell and Lynne Thomas, making their international debuts for England, scored unbeaten hundreds against an International XI in Brighton in a stand of 246, a record that stood for a quarter of a century. Lord's hosted its first women's Test match in 1979 between England and Australia. One-Day International cricket has been played by Australia, Denmark, England, India, Ireland, Japan, Netherlands, New Zealand, Pakistan, Scotland, South Africa, Sri Lanka, and the West Indies, with Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago, and International XIs participating in World Cups. A total of 707 ODIs have been played by the end of the 2009 World Cup. The 455 for 5, achieved by New Zealand Women against Pakistan Women at Hagley Oval, Christchurch in 1996/97, remains the highest team score, while the Netherlands Women were bowled out for just 22 against West Indies Women at Sportpark Het Schootsveld in Deventer in 2008. The Women's Cricket Association handed over the management of women's cricket in England to the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) in 1998. In 2005, after the eighth Women's World Cup, the International Women's Cricket Council was officially integrated into the International Cricket Council, and an ICC Women's Cricket Committee was formed to oversee women's cricket. The 2009 World Cup, the first held under ICC auspices, was won by England, the first English team of either sex to win an ICC competition. Women's teams were the first to play an international Twenty20 match, with England facing New Zealand at Hove in 2004. The first tie in a one-day international occurred between women's teams when New Zealand tied the first match of the 1982 World Cup against England, who later tied against Australia. Female wicket-keepers were the first to record six dismissals in a one-day international, with New Zealand's Sarah Illingworth and India's Venkatacher Kalpana each accounting for six batsmen on the same day in the 1993 World Cup, and Belinda Clark, former Australian captain, is the only female player to have scored a double century in an ODI, recording an unbeaten 229 against Denmark in the 1997 World Cup. Pakistan's Sajjida Shah is the youngest player to appear in international cricket, playing against Ireland four months after her 12th birthday, and also holds the record for the best bowling figures in a one-day international, taking 7 wickets for 4 runs against Japan Women at Sportpark Drieburg in Amsterdam in 2003. Fast bowler Cathryn Fitzpatrick of Australia took 180 wickets in her one-day international career. In 2009, England batsman Claire Taylor was named one of Wisden's five cricketers of the year, the first woman to receive the honor in its 120-year history. Since at least 2017, the England and Wales Cricket Board has promoted a short-form variant known as women's softball cricket, played in several county leagues in England, while the traditional game is sometimes referred to as "women's hardball cricket," requiring a distinction between the two.
